extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, game designers, and readers interested in East Asian narrative structure and storytelling techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for composing or analysing narratives using the East Asian four-part structure (ki/ introduction, shō/ development, ten/ twist, ketsu/ conclusion) across media (poetry, prose, manga, games, essays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kishōtenketsu (four-part structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes the four-part structure of many classic Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese narratives summarized as: introduction, development, twist or reversal, and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a narrative structure distinct from Western conflict-centered structures; applicable across poetry, prose, yonkoma manga, documents, dissertations, music, sentences, chapters, clauses, and game design. Emphasis is on sequence: establish → develop → turn → conclude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ki / qi / khởi — Introduction (start)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction: introduces characters, era, reasons something begins, and other information required to understand the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Chinese qǐ it usually means the reason a thing begins; in Japanese ki it introduces characters/era; in Vietnamese khởi/khai introduces the idea of the poem. Serves to set context rather than present conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shō / chéng / thừa — Development (handling/process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Development: follows leads toward the twist; expands the idea or emotional flow introduced in the first part; usually no major changes yet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chinese chéng is handling/process/hardships; Korean seung is beginning of the action often toward self-realization rather than problem-solving; Vietnamese thừa expands the introduced idea. It prepares material that the twist will redirect or contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten / zhuǎn / chuyển — Twist / turning point
rubrics_metrics.description: Twist: the story turns toward an unexpected development; the crux or climax (yama). This is the turning point that changes direction, and if multiple turns exist it is the biggest one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chinese zhuǎn means turn/crescendo; Korean jeon is reversal/change in direction; Vietnamese chuyển is the turning point. The twist may deliberately withhold a major element until this third act and can change the perceived genre of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ketsu / hé / hợp — Conclusion (result)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusion: wraps up the story and expresses result, consequence, or lessons gained through the process or results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chinese hé means result; Korean gyeol concludes and lets lessons be gained; Vietnamese hợp concludes the idea. Also called ochi in Japanese; the conclusion typically ties together prior parts rather than introducing new major developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-conflict-centric structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Kishōtenketsu as a narrative structure does not center on conflict as part of its structure, especially compared to common Western structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often described as 'without conflict' though works using kishōtenketsu can and often do contain conflict (e.g., Parasite). The emphasis is on juxtaposition, development, and twist rather than escalating antagonistic conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delayed revelation / withhold major element until third act
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately hold back a major story element until the third of four acts, which often changes the genre of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This withholding creates the dramatic turn (ten) and can be used to reframe prior material; it's a defining feature distinguishing it from more symmetrical Western structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition length flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitions between parts can be anything from a sentence to a full paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with structures like the five-paragraph essay where one sentence is encouraged for transitions. Writers may use short or extended transitions according to needs; a callback to the beginning can also be set up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion brevity (do not linger on ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusion is said to need to be quick and one should not linger long on that part of the essay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrap up promptly after the twist; prolonged denouement is discouraged in the essay/formal usages described.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Height of bumps' variability (degree of buildup to the twist)
rubrics_metrics.description: The magnitude or intensity of the buildup leading to the twist can vary from story to story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories may have subtle or pronounced lead-ups to the ten; authors can adjust the 'bumps' depending on pacing and desired effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability across scales and media
rubrics_metrics.description: Kishōtenketsu can be applied to four-panel (yonkoma) manga, stories, documents, dissertations, music, sentences, chapters, clauses, and game level design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same four-part logic at different granularities (line, sentence, paragraph, chapter) and across media; designers like Nintendo's Miyamoto have employed the idea in game level design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use for structuring arguments and essays
rubrics_metrics.description: The same pattern can be used for arguments: introduce context, develop background, introduce an unexpected contrast or insight, then conclude with synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: an essay about photocopying—ki sets historical practice, shō introduces copying machines, ten contrasts with walking/cars tradeoffs, ketsu concludes with tradeoff insight. This shows mapping of informational/argumentative flow to the four parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese regional gloss: qǐchéngzhuǎnhé (qi/chéng/zhuǎn/hé)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chinese terminology maps to: qi (start/introduction), chéng (handling/process/hardships), zhuǎn (turn/crescendo), hé (result).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical use in Chinese poetry and essays; original meanings (e.g., qi = reason a thing begins) inform how to deploy each part in Chinese-derived practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Korean regional gloss: giseungjeongyeol (gi/seung/jeon/gyeol)
rubrics_metrics.description: Korean terms map to: gi (raising issues and introducing characters), seung (beginning of the action often for self-realization), jeon (a reversal or change in direction), gyeol (conclusion and lessons gained).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Korean usage emphasizes self-realization rather than problem-solving in the second part and frames the conclusion as lesson-bearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vietnamese regional gloss: khởi–thừa–chuyển–hợp
rubrics_metrics.description: Vietnamese mapping: khởi/khai (introduce the idea), thừa (expand the idea and emotional flow), chuyển (turn/ crescendo), hợp (conclude the idea of the poem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly associated with tứ tuyệt poems; each line of the four-line poem corresponds to the four parts.
